skill_levels.looks_like: One-syllable verbs that just add -s, -ed or -ing; no letter changes.
Verbs ending in e: drop the e before -ing, add only -d for -ed.
Short-vowel verbs that double the last consonant before -ed or -ing.
Mixed rules in one sentence: the child chooses the rule, including y to ied and -es after ch, sh or x.
Short words, two sound groups or three choices, with a key word that shows each sound.

rule.support: a key word shows each sound

skill_levels.looks_like: Short everyday words, up to six to sort, no picture help; the child hears the sound alone.
Three sound groups for one spelling, or finding the word whose letters say a different sound.

rule.focus: one spelling, two or three sounds

skill_levels.looks_like: Less familiar words; the child spots a word sorted into the wrong sound group and picks it out.

rule.context: less familiar words, finding the mistake

skill_levels.looks_like: A short, familiar sentence and two words to choose from that sound the same.
A longer everyday sentence and three look-alike or sound-alike words; the child reads alone.
Sentences of eight words or more with three close choices, such as through, though and thought.
Long sentences in less familiar settings with four close choices; only the meaning tells them apart.
Two-syllable words, split for the child, or three words that start the same and a short sentence.

rule.support: the word is printed in its parts

skill_levels.looks_like: Three-syllable everyday words; the child joins the parts or reads the word in a sentence alone.
Longer words of three or four syllables; the child splits, reads and checks the word fits the sentence.
Unfamiliar long words from other subjects; the child fixes a word read or written with a part missing.
Short words that start with the k sound: c or k, with a word bank or the word said in a sentence.

rule.support: word bank or the word said aloud

skill_levels.looks_like: Short words that end in the k sound: ck after a short vowel, k after a consonant.
Words ending in the j or k sound: dge or ck after a short vowel, ge or k otherwise, four groups mixed.

rule.focus: choosing by the letters around the sound

skill_levels.looks_like: Longer, less familiar words of two syllables where the child must choose dge, ge or ck alone.
The root and the prefix or suffix are printed; the child joins them with no letter change.
Roots that need no change, with in- and -ment added; the child also matches each word to its meaning.
Roots ending in a consonant and y: the y changes to i before -ness, -less or -ment.
Longer roots, a double letter where root and suffix meet, and fixing a word another child spelt wrong.

rule.context: less familiar roots, finding and fixing the mistake

skill_levels.looks_like: A short sentence and a box of two words: to or two, to or too.
A longer sentence and all three of to, two and too, or right, write and rite, to choose from.
No word box: the child writes the homophone, or finds and fixes the one wrong word in a sentence.

rule.focus: to, two, too; right, write; there, their, they're

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer sentence or two with two or three wrong homophones to find and fix, and correct words left alone.

rule.context: more than one mistake to find

skill_levels.looks_like: Two short, familiar words printed with a plus sign; the child joins them into one compound word.
Common tricky words said aloud in a sentence, and a longer compound built from a clue.
Words with a silent letter or an unusual part, such as Wednesday and cupboard, said aloud or joined.
Long compounds with a double letter where words meet, and fixing a tricky word another child spelt wrong.

rule.context: long words, finding and fixing the mistake

skill_levels.looks_like: A familiar root with one prefix or suffix, in a short sentence; three meanings to choose from.

rule.support: a short familiar word in a short sentence

skill_levels.looks_like: A root with two parts added, such as a prefix and a suffix, in a longer everyday sentence; read alone.
Unfamiliar long words where the root changes its spelling; the sentence is used to check the meaning; four choices.
Rare long words in new contexts: finding the root of a three-part word, fixing a wrong split, working out the meaning.

rule.context: rare words, a wrong split to fix

skill_levels.looks_like: Two-syllable everyday words with the strong beat first; the word is printed in its parts and read aloud.
Two- and three-syllable words where the strong beat may come later; also finding the weak syllable.
Three- and four-syllable words: the child finds the one strong syllable among several weak ones, alone.
Words in a sentence where the meaning moves the strong beat, such as a noun and verb spelt the same.
Two words that sound the same, in a short familiar sentence, with both words printed to choose from.
Near-alike pairs such as then and than, in a longer sentence; the child chooses alone by meaning.
Three look-alike or sound-alike words to choose from, such as quiet, quite and quit, in a longer sentence.
Less common near-alike pairs in long sentences, often with no word bank: the child writes the word the meaning needs.

rule.context: less common pairs, no word bank

skill_levels.looks_like: Short words with a silent k, w or b at the start or end, with a word bank or the silent letter named.

rule.support: word bank or the group named

skill_levels.looks_like: Words where the short u sound is spelt o or ou, such as month and touch, written alone.

rule.focus: o and ou for the short u sound

skill_levels.looks_like: Mixed: silent letters and the vowel changes after w (wa, war, wor), written alone in a sentence.

rule.focus: vowel sounds after w, silent letters

skill_levels.looks_like: Rarer silent letters (g, t, h, n) in longer words, written from a sentence read aloud or sorted by the letter not said.
Nouns that add -s, or -es after s, x, ch or sh; the singular word is printed.
Nouns ending in y: keep the y after a vowel and add -s, or change y to -ies after a consonant.
Nouns ending in f or fe that change to -ves, written alone and fixed in a sentence.
All the rules mixed, with o to -oes and f words that keep -s; two or three mistakes to find and fix in a sentence.
The prefix trans- or pre- added to a short root that does not change; the root is printed.
The suffix -ion or -ous added to a root that keeps its spelling, such as collect and poison.
Roots that change before -ion, -ation or -ous: drop the e, or change y to i, written alone.
Choosing between -ion and -ation, and roots that change, in less familiar words, with a mistake to avoid.
One short sentence with a clear clue, and there, their and they're printed to choose from.

rule.support: word bank of the three words

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer sentence, no word bank; or one wrong word to find and fix in a sentence.
Two mistakes in a sentence, mixing there, their and they're with your and you're; the child works alone.
A short paragraph with three or four mistakes among correct uses; changing a right word counts as a new mistake.

rule.context: correct uses left in on purpose

skill_levels.looks_like: Short ear words with two sounds, four words to sort, or a choice of two spellings.

rule.support: two spellings printed, or a sound picture for each group

skill_levels.looks_like: Common -ough words with two sounds, such as enough and bought, written alone in a sentence.
Eight -ough words in four sounds; less common words like dough, cough and drought, written alone.
Mixed and unfamiliar words, ear in four sounds or -ough in thorough and drought, with no clue to the sound.
The rule is shown with two or three examples; the child uses it on one new short word or spots the misfit.

rule.support: the pattern is printed with examples

skill_levels.looks_like: Four examples and no rule given: the child picks the rule they show, then uses it on a new word.
The child finds the rule from a set, spots the word that breaks it, and tests it on a word that does not fit.
Longer, less familiar words: the exceptions to a rule, such as doubling in two-syllable words or keeping ee before -ing.
Common tricky words of five to seven letters, said in a short sentence, then said again in parts.

rule.support: the educator says the word in parts

skill_levels.looks_like: Seven to nine letter tricky words alone in a sentence, or one misspelt word to find and fix.
Longer words with a hidden syllable, such as February, alone; or two misspelt words in a sentence to fix.
A whole dictated sentence with a hard word, or a short passage with three or four misspelt words among correct ones.
Two families of common words with one ending each (help, care), four words, and a look-alike word to spot.
Roots with a prefix or a suffix (act, cover), six words in two families, and the family's shared meaning.
Three families from roots like tele, graph and port, a person word built from a root, and what a root means.
Unfamiliar roots such as struct, vis and aqua, longer built words, and a look-alike that shares letters but not meaning.
Four words, each starting with a different letter, with an alphabet strip printed to help.
Five words, two of which share a first letter, so one pair needs the second letter; no strip.
Six words that all start with the same letter, ordered by the second letter, or a gap on a dictionary page.
Longer, less familiar words where the third letter may decide, or a list with one word in the wrong place.
A familiar topic such as food or plants, with a word bank of three to choose from.
Weather and food words: match three words to their meanings, or choose from a bank of four.
Habitat words used exactly: match four words to meanings, or choose from a bank of five close words.
An unfamiliar topic, the water cycle or how plants make food, with longer clues and a wrong word to fix.
One short familiar sentence with the clue in the same sentence; three meanings to choose from.
Two sentences; the clue is in the sentence after the new word; three meanings to choose from.
A story passage; clues spread across sentences; choose from four meanings or explain the meaning and its clue.
A longer information passage on an unfamiliar subject; explain meanings, use the clues, and check a wrong meaning.
One short sentence; tick the word that means the same as the underlined word from three choices.
A sentence with a gap; choose a stronger word than big, nice or good from a box of four.
A story passage; find and copy the word that means the same as a given word, with no choices.
A longer passage where good has different meanings; choose the synonym that fits each use, or copy two synonyms.
A short sentence with one describing word to underline, or one word to add from a box of three.

rule.support: box of three words to add

skill_levels.looks_like: A sentence with two or three describing words to find, or a plain sentence to improve with no box.
A longer sentence with up to five describing words, or two plain nouns to turn into picture-making noun phrases.
Sentences from a descriptive passage about a trip, and a dull sentence to make as strong as the writer's.
Familiar animal and home sounds; choose the sound word from a box of three.
One sound word to underline in a short sentence, or one to choose from a box of four.
A longer sentence with two sound words to find among names of sounds and actions, or a box of four.
Sentences from a story full of sounds; find the sound verbs and choose the one that fits the writer's thing.
Two groups only, when and where; four short openers to sort, or three openers to tick from.
Three groups, when, where and how; six openers to sort, or tick the opener that tells how.
Two linked sentences: choose or write the opener that joins the second sentence to the first.
A short run of sentences: find the opener that breaks the order, fix it, or start with how.
A clear clue such as softly or across the field; choose the speech verb from a box of three.
The clue is in the spoken words, a joke, an answer or a moan; tick one of three speech verbs.
The clue is in the sentence before the speech; choose from four close speech verbs.
Say what a speech verb tells us about the speaker, or fix a speech verb the writer got wrong.
Three or four short words sharing their first two letters; the third letter decides, and it is underlined.
Five words with the same first two letters and nothing underlined: the child finds the third letter alone.
Five or six words alike for three letters, so the fourth decides; and guide words at the top of a dictionary page.
Six words alike for four letters or more, a short word that begins a longer one, and fixing a list put in the wrong order.

rule.context: glossary words and a child's list to fix

skill_levels.looks_like: A short sentence about a familiar topic with a word bank of three; only one word belongs to the topic.
Four topic words to match to their meanings, or a gap with four words from the same topic to choose between.
A longer sentence and a bank of five topic words, several with close meanings; the child picks the exact one.
A less familiar topic and no word bank: the child writes the exact topic word, or tells apart words with very close meanings.
One familiar sentence with a strong clue close to the new word; the child picks the synonym from three words.

rule.clues: one clue next to the word

skill_levels.looks_like: The child writes their own word for the new word; the clue is in the same sentence.
Two sentences: the clue is in the next sentence or comes after but or so, and the child writes their own synonym.
A longer text where the clues are spread over several sentences; the synonym must also be the right kind of word for the gap.
A short familiar story; the child copies or ticks one strong word the writer used, and the question says where to look.

rule.support: the question points to the sentence

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer recount: copy two strong words, or choose a better word or phrase for nice or a lot of.
A full story: copy strong verbs from it, and rewrite its own sentences with a stronger word for got or nice.
A long letter full of overused words: the child finds them unaided, rewrites with better choices and collects useful words.

rule.context: an unfamiliar letter with no words pointed out

skill_levels.looks_like: Three well-known adjectives to order from weakest to strongest, or a gap with two words where the clue is plain.
Three or four adjectives or adverbs to order with no help, or a gap where a clue such as only a little shows the strength.
Four words, adjectives or adverbs, with close meanings to order alone; a gap of four close words where only one fits exactly.
A scale of five words, and fixing a word that is too strong or too weak in a child's sentence.

rule.focus: finding and fixing the wrong strength

skill_levels.looks_like: One short sentence with one simile or one alliteration; the child underlines it or ticks the picture it gives.
Two or three sentences: find a simile with like, tell alliteration from rhyme, and say in a sentence what a simile shows.
A whole story with several similes, alliteration and a like that is not a simile: find each one and explain its picture or sound.
An unfamiliar poem: find two similes in one verse, choose the alliteration that copies a sound, and explain why a simile was chosen.

rule.context: a poem the child has not read

skill_levels.looks_like: Finish a simile or an alliterative phrase about something familiar by choosing from a word bank of three.
Write a whole simile or a run of alliteration into a short plain sentence about a familiar thing.
Write a fresh simile and a phrase with alliteration of your own for a scene, and pick the comparison that fits a sound.
Fix a simile that does not fit, write alliteration that copies a sound, and choose a comparison that suits the mood.
A short familiar sentence with a plain verb; the child picks the stronger verb from three.
Two sentences with a clue about mood or speed; the child chooses the strong verb that fits from four close verbs.

rule.clues: mood or speed in the first sentence

skill_levels.looks_like: The child explains in a sentence or two what a strong verb adds to the picture, or chooses it from four.
A long story mixing plain and strong verbs: replace a plain one, choose from close verbs, and compare the effect of two verbs.
Short forms made with not, such as isn't and wasn't; three to match, with the two full words printed in a box to choose from.
Short forms made with am, are, is and will, such as I'm and we're; four to match or choose, on their own.
A short form read inside a sentence, including have and should forms; says the two words it stands for and the letter left out.
Short forms beside words that sound the same, such as who's and whose, it's and its; the child decides which one means two words.
Two words ending in not, such as is not; the child writes the short form, with the ending n't shown in a box as a help.
Two words with am, are or will, such as we are; the child writes the short form alone, with no help.
Writes the short form for words inside a sentence, or fixes one or two short forms written wrongly in a sentence.
Finds and fixes two or three wrong short forms in a longer sentence, including soundalikes such as its and were.

rule.context: soundalike words and missing apostrophes mixed

skill_levels.looks_like: One short sentence, a statement or a question that starts with a question word; the child adds the end mark and a capital.
One sentence of any kind, including exclamations that start with What or How and questions with no question word.
Two sentences of different kinds run together; the child adds both end marks and the capital letter that starts the second.
Two or three sentences with tricky cases: a statement holding a question word, a question with no question word, then an exclamation.

rule.text_kind: two or three sentences without marks

skill_levels.looks_like: One sentence with its end mark: the child says whether it is a statement or a question, two kinds only.

rule.support: two kinds only, end mark printed

skill_levels.looks_like: One sentence of any of the four kinds, with a clear clue: a question word, a bossy verb first, or What a.

rule.clues: question word, bossy verb, What or How

skill_levels.looks_like: Sentences read in a short story, including a command that ends with an exclamation mark; the child names each kind.
Tricky sentences out of a story: a statement with a question word, a polite command, a question with no question word.
One speaker, spoken words first, then said and a name; speech marks printed for reading, and the comma given for writing.
One speaker, the spoken words first or last, including a question or an exclamation; the child adds every mark alone.
A short story with two or three speakers; the child finds each one's words and punctuates a line taken from the story.
A longer story where speech is split by said, and some talk is only reported; the child marks only the spoken words.
Changes one short sentence into another kind, with the first word given, such as Is for a question or What for an exclamation.
Writes one or two sentences of a named kind for a simple need, such as the question a friend asks, with no first word given.
Writes three sentences for a real purpose: commands for a recipe, questions for an interview, or a notice using three kinds.
Rewrites a dull or muddled text, choosing which kinds of sentence suit it, or writes a story opening using all four kinds.

rule.focus: choosing the kind for its effect

skill_levels.looks_like: One short sentence with a clear time word such as yesterday or tomorrow; three verb forms to choose from.
The child writes the past of a verb alone in one sentence; regular verbs and a common irregular one.
Past, present and future written alone, irregular verbs included, and one slip of tense found and fixed in a sentence.
A short story in the past with speech in another tense: keep the story steady and leave the speech as spoken.
Is or are after one clear subject in a short sentence; two choices.
Was or were, has or have, chosen alone; subjects joined with and, or a pronoun such as we.
Is, are, was, were, has or have in longer sentences, including everyone, and one wrong verb found and fixed.
Subjects split from their verb by other words, such as the box of sweets; two wrong verbs to find and fix.

rule.context: a noun between subject and verb

skill_levels.looks_like: A short sentence with a familiar joining word such as because, but or before; find it or pick it from three.
Less familiar connectives such as unless, while and so that, found or chosen alone in one sentence.
Longer sentences with two connectives to find, a best-fit choice from four, and two sentences joined in writing.
A five-paragraph recount: find the links between paragraphs, swap one for a word of the same meaning, write a new opener.
Many or much in a short familiar sentence, with a two-word box to choose from.
Every, few or little chosen from a box of three, where the noun shows whether one or many is meant.
No word box for the gaps: the child writes a quantifier that fits the noun, or chooses from four.
Unfamiliar notices, recipes and reports: four close choices where the meaning of the sentence before decides the answer.
One adverb ending in -ly that tells how, in a short sentence with a clear action verb.
Single adverbs of how, when and where, with and without -ly, found or sorted alone.
Adverbial phrases such as after lunch or under the tree, found and sorted, and added to an instruction.
A full set of instructions: find and sort the adverbs and phrases, then rewrite a vague step so a reader can follow it.
Two short statements run together; the child adds one full stop and one capital letter.
A question and a statement run together; the child chooses between the question mark and the full stop.
Three or four sentences with no breaks shown, mixing statements, questions and exclamations.
A longer run with traps such as asked why and wondered whether, and wrong marks to find and fix.
A list of three things in a short sentence: add the commas, or tick the sentence that has them right.
One comma after an opening phrase, or before the name of the person spoken to, in a short sentence.
Two kinds of comma in one sentence, and choosing the sentence whose comma gives the meaning asked for.
Three commas in a longer sentence, a name that is not spoken to, and how a comma changes what a list means.
The speech marks are already there; the child adds the comma and full stop to one short statement.
One speaker, a statement: the child adds the speech marks, the comma and the end mark alone.
A question or an exclamation inside the speech marks, with asked or shouted after them.
Two speakers in a short conversation: speech marks, inside marks and a new line for each new speaker.
One owner named in the question: write 's on the owner word, or tick it.
Many owners whose word ends in s: write or tick the apostrophe after the s.
One owner or many, decided from the sentence, including children's; one missing apostrophe found and fixed.
Longer sentences mixing owners with plain plurals: two mistakes to fix, and the meaning of the apostrophe explained by choosing.
A short, familiar story; the question names the key word, and the answer is a word or phrase in one sentence.

rule.support: key word given in the question

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer information text; the child scans alone for the key word and copies or picks the exact words.

rule.clues: the question word appears in the passage

skill_levels.looks_like: A recount with several similar facts close together; the child picks the right one and answers in a sentence using the text.

rule.focus: near-miss facts sit next to the answer

skill_levels.looks_like: An unfamiliar leaflet; the question uses different words from the text, and the answer joins two facts or gives the reason stated.
A short story about one character; the child copies the words that describe them and says if they show kind or unkind.

rule.support: the trait to look for is named

skill_levels.looks_like: A short description of a busy place; the child copies the words for one sense and says how a character feels there.
A story with a place and a person both described; the child finds the words and explains what they show, alone.

rule.focus: words that build a character and a setting

skill_levels.looks_like: An unfamiliar coastal story where the place and the character change; the child explains each change with words from both parts.
A short familiar story; three events to number, and one plain cause to choose.
A recount with time words such as first and after; up to four events and a cause the text states with because.
A story without time words to lean on; five events to order and the earlier event that caused a later one.
A longer story; six events to order, a chain of cause and result, and finding the swap in someone else's order.
One short blurb; the child picks the reader it suits and says if it is a story or facts.
Two blurbs side by side, one story and one information book; the child matches each to a reader, alone.
A blurb and a child's review; the child chooses for a reader and explains with one detail from the text.
Two blurbs and a librarian's review in less familiar kinds of book; the child explains why one book suits a reader and one does not.
A five-line contents page; the child finds the chapter and picks its page from a word bank.
An eight-line index in alphabetical order, one page for each entry; the child finds the page alone.
An index where entries have two or three pages; the child writes every page and chooses contents or index for a task.
The question's words are not in the index; the child picks the entry that means the same and spots a misread line.

rule.context: the key word is not listed

skill_levels.looks_like: A short familiar passage where every sentence is about one topic; the child picks the main point from three.
An information passage with clear details; the child picks the main point or title, alone, and writes it in one sentence.

rule.focus: main point or a small detail

skill_levels.looks_like: A recount whose first sentence is only a detail; the child finds and writes the main point, leaving out small details.

rule.focus: the main point is not in the first line

skill_levels.looks_like: An unfamiliar two-paragraph information text; the child gives the point of each paragraph and fixes someone's wrong main point.
A short familiar story with two or three clear clues close together; the child picks a feeling from a few given words.
A longer story with clues spread out; feelings change once, and the child works alone with three choices or one sentence.
A full story where a character hides a feeling; the child explains thoughts and reasons from what the character does and says.
A story in an unfamiliar place where a character says one thing and feels another; the child explains, and fixes a wrong reading.

rule.context: a new city; words and actions disagree

skill_levels.looks_like: A very short story with one clear lesson that is almost said; the child picks it from three choices or writes one sentence.
A short story whose lesson is not said; the child names it alone and matches it to another story with the same lesson.

rule.focus: naming the lesson; one matching story

skill_levels.looks_like: A full fable where the lesson must be worked out from the whole story; the child names it, gives a reason and finds a story sharing it.

rule.focus: the grade's target: theme with a reason

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer story whose lesson is hidden in a change of mind; the child explains it and corrects someone else's wrong idea of the theme.

rule.context: the theme is never said; a wrong reading to fix

skill_levels.looks_like: Two very short tellings side by side that differ in one detail; the child fills two boxes or picks from three choices.

rule.support: the tellings are labelled and short

skill_levels.looks_like: Two tellings with the same beginning and middle but different endings; the child works alone and finds what is the same and what changes.
Two tellings that change the characters, the place and the ending; the child compares several details and explains one change.

rule.focus: the grade's target: several sames and changes

skill_levels.looks_like: Two tellings from different times and places; the child explains why details changed and fixes a wrong comparison.

rule.context: when and where each telling was written

skill_levels.looks_like: A short familiar story that stops just before a clear ending; the child picks the likely ending from three choices.
A story that follows a well-known pattern, a kindness repaid; the child predicts alone and names the clue.
A full story much like a story the child knows; the child predicts the ending and gives a reason from the story or the other story.

rule.focus: the grade's target: prediction from known stories

skill_levels.looks_like: A mystery story with clues and a false lead; the child predicts the ending, judges another child's prediction and explains.

rule.context: a mystery; checking someone else's prediction

skill_levels.looks_like: A short recipe with numbered steps and a list of things needed; the child orders or checks two or three steps.
Numbered steps with direction words such as left, right and second; the child follows them alone and says where they lead.
Steps written as sentences with time words such as before and after, not in doing order; the child works out the real order alone.

rule.focus: the grade's target: time words decide the order

skill_levels.looks_like: A word puzzle where each step changes the last result; the child follows it, finds which step someone missed and fixes it.

rule.context: steps build on each other; finding a missed step

skill_levels.looks_like: A short advert with clear opinion words like best and sweetest; the child sorts four sentences or picks one.

rule.support: opinion words are easy to spot

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer recount mixing facts and opinions; the child sorts five or six sentences alone.
An information text where some opinions have no I think and sound sure; the child sorts every sentence alone.

rule.focus: the grade's target: opinions that sound like facts

skill_levels.looks_like: An unfamiliar letter where facts and opinions sit side by side; the child sorts them, checks another child's sorting and fixes it.

rule.context: a letter to a newsletter; correcting a sort

skill_levels.looks_like: A short, familiar text or a contents page; the question uses the passage's own words, and the answer sits in one sentence.

rule.support: the question repeats the passage's words

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer information text read alone; the question uses different words from the passage, and the answer is in one place.
A full story read alone; some answers need two places in the text, put together in the child's own sentence.
A long letter about an unfamiliar place; the child explains a reason by joining two points and rejects close wrong answers.
A short, familiar story about one person; the question names the quality, and the child copies the words that show it.

rule.support: the quality is named in the question

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer text about a place and a person, read alone; the child finds a phrase for a named sense or quality.
A full story read alone; the child explains how a character is built and quotes the key words, with no quality given.
A long story in an unfamiliar place whose mood changes; the child explains how chosen words build each mood and the change.

rule.context: unfamiliar place, a setting that changes

skill_levels.looks_like: A short familiar story with three stages; each stage name comes with a hint saying what it does.

rule.support: each stage name has a hint

skill_levels.looks_like: A familiar story with five short paragraphs, one stage each; stage names without hints.
A full story or a report read alone; the child places every part in its stage, from opening to ending or introduction to conclusion.
A report printed out of order, or a story that starts with its problem; the child sorts out the true stages.
One short, familiar paragraph with its main point in the first sentence; choose from three printed phrases.
Two paragraphs read alone, each with its own main point; the child separates the point from colourful details.
Three paragraphs read alone; a main point may come at the end, and four close choices include first words and details.
A long text on an unfamiliar topic; the child picks the key words for notes, including a point stated only at a paragraph's end.
One short, familiar paragraph with a clear title; three choices, one of them obviously a small detail.

rule.support: a title that names the topic

skill_levels.looks_like: Three short paragraphs read alone; the child uses first sentences to get the gist and match headings.
Five paragraphs read alone, with a title that hints but does not name the topic; four close choices, including one too wide.
A long text about an unfamiliar place whose title misleads; the child finds the true gist and judges a better title.
A short, familiar recount whose sentences start with time links; the child is told how many to find.

rule.support: the number of links is given

skill_levels.looks_like: A short story read alone; links inside sentences show reason, result, contrast and adding, and the child names each job.
Four paragraphs read alone; links between paragraphs and sentences, no count given, and the child says how each point builds on the last.
A long text on an unfamiliar topic; links include longer phrases and words that point back, and the child explains what each link does.
A short, familiar school story; three options or a box of feeling words to choose from.

rule.support: feeling words given in a box

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer story in a less familiar place; the child works out the setting and picks the clue alone.

rule.clues: two or three clues close together

skill_levels.looks_like: A full story; the child explains what a character's actions suggest and quotes the clue, with no options.
An unfamiliar way of life; the child judges another reader's wrong idea and explains, quoting clues.

rule.focus: checking an inference against the text

skill_levels.looks_like: A short, familiar story; the clue sits right before the end and three endings are given.
A longer story; the child predicts alone and names the earlier event that points to it.

rule.clues: a clue earlier in the story

skill_levels.looks_like: A clue planted early in a longer story; the child predicts and explains the link in writing.

rule.clues: a clue planted at the start

skill_levels.looks_like: Several clues in a long story; the child judges between endings and explains why one prediction is unlikely.

rule.clues: several clues, some pointing the wrong way

skill_levels.looks_like: Two very short familiar texts with one clear shared lesson; options and a word bank are given.
Two short texts of different kinds; the child names the shared theme and one difference alone.
A tale and a recount on one theme; the child compares the theme and the features of each.
A poem and an information leaflet; the child explains why sharing a topic is not sharing a theme.
A short story of a grandparent's childhood; each question names the one thing to find.

rule.support: the question names the detail to copy

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer story set in a different part of India today; the child finds place details alone.
A story set in a named year; the child finds time details and explains how life then differs from now.

rule.context: a named year in the past

skill_levels.looks_like: An unfamiliar time and place with one detail that does not fit; the child spots it and explains.

rule.focus: finding a detail that cannot belong

skill_levels.looks_like: Short familiar stories with I or he and she on every line; two options to choose from.

rule.support: two options; the pronouns are printed in the options

skill_levels.looks_like: Longer stories, including one told by we; the child finds the narrator word alone.
Stories where characters say I inside speech marks; the child looks only outside the speech.
Unusual narrators, such as an object, or a long story inside a story; the child explains the choice.

rule.focus: a narrator who speaks mostly of others

skill_levels.looks_like: A short familiar story; a sentence starter is given and the child links one feeling to one memory.
A longer story about a place; the child compares the setting with a place they know, alone.

rule.focus: linking a setting to their own life

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer story with a turning point; the child explains a feeling about a character and links it to their life.

rule.focus: linking a character and an event to their own life

skill_levels.looks_like: A character from an unfamiliar way of life; the child explains how their view changed and why.
A short advert; four sentences to sort, each opinion marked by I think, tastiest or love.
A longer advert; six sentences to sort, with marker words such as in our opinion and best.
A review by a child; sentences mix facts about a show with opinions, marked by in my view or should.
A review where facts sound like praise and opinions have no I think; the child sorts and explains.

rule.focus: facts that sound good, opinions without marker words

skill_levels.looks_like: One short familiar sentence; find one kind of word at a time, nouns or verbs, with the kind named.

rule.support: one word kind at a time, everyday words

skill_levels.looks_like: A longer sentence, alone; find pronouns or adjectives, or sort words into noun, verb and adjective.
Sentences taken from a story; find verbs or pronouns and sort words into all four kinds.
An information text with words that can do two jobs, such as plant, water and light; the child decides the job here.

rule.focus: a word whose job depends on the sentence

skill_levels.looks_like: Words that tell where, in one short sentence, chosen from a box of three.

rule.support: word bank of three; place words only

skill_levels.looks_like: Words that tell when, such as on, at and in, chosen from a box of four.
No word bank: the child writes or finds words such as during, until, since and under.
Choosing between words close in meaning, such as through or across, between or among, when or where.
One short sentence with a time word such as yesterday or every day; two choices, or four verbs to sort.

rule.clues: a time word in the sentence

skill_levels.looks_like: No time word next to the verb: keep the second verb in the tense of the first; fix one slip.
A short paragraph in one tense; fix two slips, and sort verbs including went and ran.
A longer recount with three slips to find and fix; spot verbs that only look past, such as need.
The most common verbs, such as go, eat and see, with the first letter of the past given.
Verbs that change one vowel, such as write and drink, in a sentence, with no letter given.
Irregular verbs in a sentence; find and fix two wrong pasts such as goed or runned.
Less common verbs such as catch, bring and teach; fix three wrong pasts in a short recount.
Two short ideas joined with and, but or so, chosen from a box of three.
Joining a cause or a condition with because or if; one rewrite joining two short sentences.
Joining words of time, such as before and after, alone; the child may change the order of the ideas.
Fixing a joining word that makes no sense, starting a sentence with If, and joining three ideas.

rule.focus: meaning of the joining word; three ideas

skill_levels.looks_like: The notes are printed in a jumbled list or the first box is done; the child puts each note in its box.

rule.support: notes printed or first box filled

skill_levels.looks_like: The child plans a familiar story or report alone: one short note for each of three boxes.
The child plans alone with a problem and how it is solved, or a report under three chosen headings.

rule.context: story with a problem, or a report

skill_levels.looks_like: An unfamiliar topic: the child chooses the parts, leaves out a note that does not fit and marks the most important point.

rule.context: unfamiliar topic or kind of text

skill_levels.looks_like: A familiar place or person with a box of describing words; the child writes two or three sentences.
A familiar place or person with no word box; three sentences with describing words chosen alone.
A story setting or character in four or five sentences, using what is seen, heard and felt.
An unfamiliar setting or character; five sentences that show a feeling through details and one comparison.
A short information text in the order of the table; two or three boxes, each fact a few words.
A longer text about three things; the child fills three boxes, finding each fact alone.
A text of five or six facts; four boxes with general labels, so the child picks the right part of each sentence.
A text comparing two things, facts mixed together; the child sorts them into a two-column table or labels a diagram.
The events are given as notes in order with a box of time words; the child writes three or four sentences.
A familiar event told in four sentences alone, with at least two different time words.
Four to six sentences of a story or a day in order, the child choosing the events and the time words.
Jumbled or unfamiliar events: the child decides the order and shows why one event leads to the next.
Two speakers and two lines of speech in the story; the child sets them out and adds a direction for each.
Two speakers, four short lines in the story; the child writes the playscript alone with two stage directions.
A story part with two or three speakers and actions; names, colons, new lines and directions, with no narrator.
The story only reports what was said; the child makes up the lines, adds a scene heading and directions showing feelings.
One short sentence, and the weak part is named for the child; the child writes it again better.
Two or three sentences with one clear weakness, such as a repeated word or 'and then'; the child finds and fixes it.
A short piece with a gap in sense or content; the child names the exact place and writes a better version.
A partner's piece with more than one weakness; the child picks the most important, says why it matters to a reader and fixes it.
A short blurb of a familiar story and sentence starters; the child says what it is about and one thing liked.
A short blurb and no starters; three sentences giving what it is about, an opinion and one reason.
A longer blurb; a review of three to five sentences with what it is about, an opinion and two reasons.
A review for a named reader: who would enjoy it, a part liked and a part not liked, with reasons.
One or two sentences with two spelling mistakes, and the child is told how many to find.
Two sentences with two or three mistakes of spelling and grammar; the number is given.
Three or four sentences with spelling, grammar and punctuation mistakes; the child finds them alone.
A longer piece with mixed mistakes, including sound-alike words and capitals; no number is given.
Three or four sentences about a familiar place or person, with a word bank and the senses to use listed.

rule.support: word bank and the senses named

skill_levels.looks_like: Four or five sentences about a familiar setting or person, alone, using at least two senses.
A paragraph, alone, with chosen details, three senses and one comparison that makes the reader want to read on.

rule.focus: senses, comparison, a hook for the reader

skill_levels.looks_like: An unfamiliar or imagined setting or character, building a mood, or saying which detail will hook the reader.
A short fable; the new ending or beginning is given its first sentence and what must change.
A longer familiar story; a new ending or beginning written alone, with what must change named.
A full story; the new opening or ending must fit the main character's personality and everything already told.

rule.focus: fits the character and the events

skill_levels.looks_like: A folk tale with a message; the ending is told by another character, changes the setting, or is explained.

rule.focus: another viewpoint or explaining the change

skill_levels.looks_like: A short information text; two or three labelled boxes, each filled with a few key words copied from it.
A longer text with extra detail; three boxes, choosing the key words that answer each label.
A full information text; three or four boxes for a set purpose, leaving out what the purpose does not need.
A long text on an unfamiliar topic; the child makes their own notes, then writes a short paragraph from them.
Four events from a short recount to number, with linking words such as first and after that as clues.
Five jumbled sentences with no passage; the linking words and what each sentence refers back to give the order.
A paragraph written from notes, ideas in order, linked by at least three different linking words.
A paragraph on causes and results, or ideas the child orders and explains, with links for time, cause and contrast.
The first lines of a scene are given; the child adds four lines for two characters with one stage direction.

rule.support: scene heading and first lines given

skill_levels.looks_like: A one-line brief; the child writes six lines for two characters with two stage directions.
An original scene for two or three characters, with a scene heading, six to eight lines and stage directions.
A story turned into a scene, or an unfamiliar setting, where stage directions show feelings the lines do not say.

rule.context: unfamiliar setting or a story to adapt

skill_levels.looks_like: A short story is given; the child fills a story plan of three labelled boxes with short notes from it.

rule.support: the story and the frame given

skill_levels.looks_like: The child plans their own piece alone, in the frame named: a story mountain, a list of steps or a mind map.
The child chooses the frame that suits the purpose, says which, and writes the plan in short notes.
An unfamiliar purpose; the child plans it, explains why the frame suits, or fixes a plan made in the wrong frame.
A short story; boxes for looks, personality, likes and a quote, each filled with words stated in the story.
A longer story; boxes ask for the detail that shows a trait, so the child finds the evidence.
A written profile of one character: looks, personality, likes and a quote, each backed by a detail from the story.
A longer story; the child infers a trait or a change, or profiles a new character to fit the next story.
Two or three sentences as a character about a familiar place, with a starter: I think … because ….
Three or four sentences as a character, alone, giving an opinion of a place or person and one reason.
A short paragraph in the character's voice giving an opinion of a setting or another character, with two reasons.
Two opposite views of one place, a strange setting, or a character whose opinion has changed, each view made clear.
A short note to a familiar reader, using a printed frame for the view and two reasons.
A note to the principal or librarian, alone, giving one view and two reasons on a school topic.
A letter, notice or newsletter piece for a named reader, with a view, two reasons with details, and fitting tone.
A speech, leaflet or letter for a wider audience that answers a point against the view or ranks the reasons.
Two or three short sentences; two or three word mistakes, and the child is told how many and of which kind.

rule.support: number and kind of mistakes given

skill_levels.looks_like: A short paragraph with three or four word mistakes, such as a verb tense or an apostrophe, found alone.
A paragraph with speech and apostrophes; four to six word mistakes plus missing capitals or commas.
A letter, report or instructions with five to seven mistakes, including homophones, and tricky words that are already right.
Two or three sentences; the weakness is pointed out, and the child rewrites one sentence to fix it.
A short paragraph; the child finds one weakness of sense, accuracy or tense alone and fixes it.
A paragraph checked for sense, accuracy and content; the child names the weakness, fixes it and says why.
A friend's longer piece with weaknesses of fact, tone or ending; the child rewrites one part and explains it for the reader.

rule.focus: explaining the change for the reader

skill_levels.looks_like: Book titles with a one-line cover note; two groups or two choices; fiction means made up.

rule.support: a one-line note about each book

skill_levels.looks_like: One or two sentences from inside a book; the child decides alone whether it is made up or true.
Places books on library shelves by subject: fiction, or a named non-fiction shelf; four to six books.
Tricky books: true diaries, stories set in real places; finds and fixes a book on the wrong shelf.

rule.context: books that look like the other kind

skill_levels.looks_like: Short cover notes or one-sentence extracts; sorts six into fiction and non-fiction, or picks one of two.

rule.support: fiction and non-fiction are explained in the question

skill_levels.looks_like: Places a non-fiction book in its numbered section; the section names are printed beside each number.
Uses spine labels: fiction by the author's surname, non-fiction by section number; six books or a label to build.
True books told like stories, stories hidden on fact shelves; finds the misplaced book and the right label.
Three kinds of story, each with one clear clue; a short extract or a feature to match.

rule.support: the kinds are named in the question

skill_levels.looks_like: Four kinds to choose from; an extract of two or three sentences; the child decides alone.
A whole short story; names its kind and gives two features from the story that show it.
Two stories side by side; compares their kinds and features and explains the difference.
Two short extracts of different kinds; one feature compared at a time, with a word bank.
Two kinds compared on characters, settings or language, from extracts of up to a hundred words; no word bank.
Two complete short stories; compares characters, settings, plots and language, with words from the stories.
Less familiar kinds such as science fiction and historical stories; tests a wrong claim and explains why.
A few lines of instructions or a recount; the purposes are said in plain words; two or three choices.
Names the purpose with its own word, instructs, reports, recounts or explains, from a short text.
A full page of report or recount; finds the purpose, the features that show it and what keeps the reader reading.
Two texts on one topic with different purposes; compares them and fixes a wrong idea about one.
Names one familiar part (title, heading, verse, stage direction) from a picture of it; three choices.
Says what a part is for, or turns a short sentence into a list with bullet points.
Works on a whole page of instructions or a playscript: says why a part is used and sets out steps with numbers.
A newsletter with mixed parts; finds a heading that does not fit, fixes a title mix-up and picks the right list.
Matches four kinds of text to their main features, or names the kind from one feature shown.
Names the kind of a short text from its features and sets out a recipe with a heading and a list.
A full playscript or set of instructions; says what each feature does and adds the headings and lists it lacks.
A long report with features used wrongly; decides which features belong, fixes them and explains the choice.
Four short sentences into two groups with the headings given, or a heading for three simple sentences.
Six sentences into two groups, or a heading or a sentence that fits a short paragraph; the child works alone.
Six sentences into three sections for a report or recount; some share a word but not an idea.
A child's two-paragraph report; finds the sentence in the wrong paragraph, picks a heading and places new sentences.
Six notes into two sections with headings given, or the odd sentence in a short paragraph.
Eight notes into three sections; the odd sentence shares the paragraph's topic word; headings matched alone.
A three-paragraph report; matches headings, finds the sentence that does not belong and places left-out sentences.
A letter whose paragraphs mix two ideas; finds where a new paragraph starts, splits it and says why each begins.
A one- or two-line advert; underlines the words that make it sound good, or says why it asks a question.

rule.support: the number of words to find is given

skill_levels.looks_like: A short advert of three or four sentences; finds strong adjectives, numbers and promises and says what they do.
A full review; tells praise from plain facts and explains two ways it persuades, with examples.
An advert and a review of the same camp; compares them, spots claims the review disagrees with, judges which to trust.
